chunks: Testing components on a board. The question: How do you test components at the board level?
When a part is soldered onto a board, a meter does not measure that part alone. It measures everything connected across it.
So a reading that looks wrong does not prove the part is bad. Testing components on a board means knowing what your meter really sees, and choosing a check that removes the doubt.
Imagine measuring how hard it is to push water through one pipe, but that pipe has a second pipe running beside it between the same two points.
Water takes both routes, so the pair looks easier to push through than your pipe alone. A meter on a board does the same thing: other parts give the current extra routes.
The analogy has a limit: the extra routes are not always obvious, because they run through other parts of the circuit.
The meter sees R x in parallel with the rest of the circuit (orange). 10 kilohms ∥ 10 kilohms reads 5 kilohms, so a good part looks 50 % low.
Resistance: how hard a part makes it for current to flow, in ohms (Ω). In parallel: connected across the same two points, so current can take either route.
In-circuit: measured while the part is still soldered on the board. Lifting a leg: unsoldering one end of a part so nothing else is across it.
4-wire (Kelvin) measurement: using separate wires to push current and to sense voltage, so lead resistance does not count.
A 10 kilohms resistor on a board has another 10 kilohms path hidden across it. Two equal resistors in parallel give half the value, so the meter reads 5 kilohms.
The resistor is perfectly good, but it looks 50 % low. A reading higher than expected would point to a bad or open part, but a lower one is ambiguous.
To settle it, lift one leg and measure again, or power the board and check the voltages and currents instead. That is the whole idea.
"On a board a meter measures everything across the part, so a 10 k resistor with a 10 k path reads 5 k.
I lift a leg or infer from powered voltages and currents; ICT uses guarding.

Capacitors get shorts and LCR/ESR checks; diodes and LEDs diode-mode; transistors junction and bias checks; crystals via a low-capacitance probe or buffered output; regulators under load; and low-value shunts with 4-wire measurement."
